text: In 1930, if you wanted to drive from San Francisco to Marin County, you took a boat. There was no other way.

Ferries had crossed the strait since the 1840s. By the twenties Southern Pacific was running the largest ferry operation in the world, and fifty thousand people a week moved through the Ferry Building.
San Francisco was the biggest city in America still dependent on boats, and it was growing more slowly than the country around it.
The idea of bridging the Golden Gate had been around since 1919. Strauss, who spent thirteen years arguing for it, called those years a war.

Southern Pacific sued. A bridge would end the ferry monopoly that made the railroad rich. The War Department worried that a collapsed span would bottle up the harbour. Conservationists said it would ruin the view. And nobody much liked the first design, a cantilever-suspension hybrid the critics called the rat-trap.

Then there was the money. In November 1930, voters across six counties agreed to put up their own homes, their farms and their business properties as collateral for a thirty-five million dollar bond. They approved it three to one.
It was the Depression. No bond house would buy. In 1932 Amadeo Giannini, of Bank of America, took six million dollars' worth, and the work could start.
The debt was cleared in 1971. Thirty-five million in principal, thirty-nine million in interest, every cent of it paid out of tolls. Nobody ever lost their farm.
The man who campaigned for the bridge was Joseph Strauss. He had built some four hundred drawbridges. He had never built a suspension span.
The structural design, the actual mathematics of it, was the work of Charles Ellis, a professor of engineering who ran the calculations by hand. Thousands of them.
In late 1931, Strauss dismissed him. He said Ellis was wasting time and money.
style: Flatter. Slower. State it plainly and do not lean on it.

text: When the bridge opened in 1937, Ellis was not mentioned. Strauss's name went on the plaque. After Strauss died, his widow paid for a statue at the San Francisco end. The inscription reads: the man who built the bridge.
Ellis was named as the designer in his obituary, in 1949. The bridge district acknowledged him formally in 2007, seventy years after it opened.
Work began in January 1933. Four thousand two hundred feet between the towers, the longest suspension span in the world, and it held that record until 1964.
The hardest part was the south tower. Its foundation had to be sunk eleven hundred feet offshore, a hundred and ten feet below the low-water mark, in open ocean.
Spinning the cables took six months and nine days. Twenty-seven thousand wires in each one. Laid end to end, enough wire to go round the earth three times.
Unemployment in San Francisco was over twenty-five per cent. The work paid between four and eleven dollars a day, and men took it.

Strauss insisted on a safety net slung under the deck. It cost a hundred and thirty thousand dollars, which at the time was thought extravagant. It caught nineteen men. They called themselves the Halfway to Hell Club.
Then, on the seventeenth of February 1937, a stripping scaffold broke loose and tore straight through the net. Ten men fell two hundred and twenty feet.
style: Slower. Grave, but not theatrical. Let the facts do it.

text: Eleven died building it. The rule of thumb in those years was one death for every million dollars spent. By that arithmetic, eleven was low.
The plaque on the bridge names Joseph Strauss. The drawings, in the Library of Congress, are signed by Charles Ellis.
style: Slow. Final. Do not rise at the end.
